description: We are a group of friends who enjoy prototyping applications in our free time.
summary: On the way to Mars and on its surface, help from Earth is up to 22 minutes away, so astronauts must catch health problems themselves. Pulsar is a crew health app that answers two questions on one screen: "Am I OK?" and "What do I do now?". It follows a crew of four in a habitat at Gale Crater with seven indicators (heart rate, blood oxygen, blood pressure, radiation, sleep, exercise and a daily wellbeing check-in). Each indicator has a traffic light based on NASA-STD-3001 and other cited standards, and each alert comes with concrete steps the crew can take without waiting for Earth. Radiation and space weather are real NASA data: what Curiosity's RAD measured at Gale Crater, and NASA DONKI. A server on the habitat's network keeps the crew's data, astronauts sign in with their face, and mission control sees the crew with the real Earth–Mars signal delay.
details:
What it does

Pulsar turns a crew's health data into one answer and one action. The crew page shows the four crew members at a glance: their status (All good / Attention / Act now), what they are doing and their most urgent alert. Each crew member's panel answers "Am I OK?" and "What do I do now?", with seven indicators, trends over 24 hours and 7 days, and a four-question daily wellbeing check-in (NASA asks for minimally obtrusive measures of psychological state on long missions, OCHMO-TB-016). Every threshold cites its source (NASA-STD-3001 technical briefs, WHO, ACC/AHA, ACSM), and when a cut-off is Pulsar's own choice, the app says so. The About page lists every rule.

How it works

- Real radiation: the habitat's dose rate replays what Curiosity's RAD instrument measured at Gale Crater (NASA PDS, sols 1780–1830). The "Solar storm" scenario replays the solar particle event of 10 September 2017, at about 2.2 times the background. The mission dose is tracked against NASA's 600 mSv career limit.

- Real space weather: coronal mass ejections, solar particle events and geomagnetic storms from NASA DONKI, with a heads-up when a CME is forecast to reach Mars within 72 hours. The NASA API key stays on our server.

- Mars time and distance: the mission sol and local solar time follow NASA GISS Mars24. Today's Earth–Mars signal delay comes from NASA JPL planet positions.

- Habitat server: it keeps check-ins and actions marked as done, and pushes every change live to all devices. If a device breaks, nothing is lost. Offline, changes wait on the device and are sent when the server is back.

- Face sign-in: each astronaut signs in with their face (face-api.js, on the device) and changes only their own data; everyone sees everyone. The picture never leaves the device: only 128 numbers that describe the face are sent.

- Mission control (/earth): sees the crew one signal delay late, receives a health report every 6 Mars hours and can download it as a PDF.

- Demo scenarios (solar storm, low cabin oxygen, fever, sleepless night, missed workouts, feeling isolated) can be shared as links.

- Built for Mars: Pulsar runs on the habitat's own server, on the station's local network, so it keeps working without Earth. On Mars, space weather and radiation would come from sources near the planet (orbiters, surface detectors) to avoid the 3–22 minute delay from Earth; in this prototype, real NASA data from Curiosity's RAD and DONKI stands in for them.

Benefits

One status and one action reduce stress and decision time when Earth cannot help right away. Trends catch slow changes. The crew sees who needs help and who is already acting.

What we hope to achieve

A clear, sourced and testable base for crew self-monitoring, ready to connect to real wearables and habitat sensors.

Tools

TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Node.js, Vitest (126 unit tests), face-api.js with TensorFlow.js, jsPDF, Nginx and Docker. It works offline, installs on phones and tablets, and comes in English and Spanish. Source code (Apache 2.0): https://github.com/catacody-startup/Pulsar-App

Prototype: vital signs are simulated; radiation and space weather are real NASA data. Not a medical device.
